The presidential candidate of the Young Progressives Party (YPP), Peter Agada, has pledged to release N40 million to each of Nigeria’s 8,809 wards every month if elected president in the 2027 general election.
Mr Agada, an architect, said the funds would serve as seed capital for grassroots development, adding that his administration would prioritise making each ward economically independent and promoting balanced economic growth across the country.
He made the pledge on Monday while appearing on Channels Television’s Politics Today, where he discussed his plans for the country if elected president.
The presidential candidate also promised to involve local professionals in executing infrastructure projects, saying his first task after inauguration would be to engage professionals to develop a master plan for each ward.
He said each ward would have a target of engaging 350 people, including architects, engineers, town planners, road construction workers, artisans, doctors and nurses.
“Like I said, every ward has a 350 person target. Now, this 350 persons as architects, engineers, town planners, road construction people, artisans, doctors, nurses. So you see, by the time you’re done setting up these ward areas and putting in that funding, because we are sending in about N40 million from our sources.
“We’re sending in N40 million to these wards every month as seed capital. You have now set up a system, an economic system that can grow on its own and make that ward an independent ward for development,” he said

The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) cleared 18 candidates for the presidential election scheduled for 16 January 2027.
Some of the other presidential hopefuls aside from Mr Agada include President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC), who is seeking a second term, Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Peter Obi of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Sandy Onor (PDP), Omoyele Sowore (AAC), former Cross River Governor Donald Duke (PRP), and Adewole Adebayo (SDP).
Mr Agada also criticised President Tinubu’s borrowings, promising that his administration would rely less on foreign loans than the incumbent government.
The presidential candidate said he was not opposed to borrowing but argued that the current administration was borrowing excessively. He added that his government would focus on reducing project costs rather than accumulating more debt.
To achieve this, he proposed establishing a National Council on Procurement to monitor the costs of government projects and ensure proper documentation.
“I would not borrow as much as they’re doing. I don’t have a problem with borrowing, all right? They are borrowing too much, and I would save costs rather than borrowing. I’ve always been an advocate for setting up the National Council on Procurement,” he said.
The YPP candidate also alleged that several projects undertaken by the Tinubu administration had been overinflated, referencing the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway as an example.
He said his administration would address the practice by ensuring proper monitoring of project costs.
The Tinubu administration, like its predecessor, has continued to rely on domestic and external loans to finance government projects, with several borrowing requests submitted to and approved by the National Assembly.
In October, President Tinubu sought the National Assembly’s approval to proceed with the processing of external loans worth $20,517,755,901 and €1,045,083,643 under the 2026–2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan.
In November, the president withdrew the request and instead requested approval for a new external borrowing plan of $7.7 billion to partly finance the 2026 budget deficit.
The request came about five months after the National Assembly approved a $516.3 million loan from Deutsche Bank AG to finance the construction of the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, a flagship infrastructure project under the administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda.
The loan has a tenure of nine years, including a grace period of up to three years, with an interest rate capped at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange’s Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) plus 5.3 per cent annually.
The facility is backed by insurance from the Islamic Corporation for the Insurance of Investment and Export Credit, the insurance arm of the Islamic Development Bank.
In March, the National Assembly also approved a $6 billion external borrowing plan for the federal government.
Of the amount, $5 billion was to be sourced from First Abu Dhabi Bank to support the national budget, while a $1 billion export finance facility from the United Kingdom, arranged by Citibank, was earmarked for the rehabilitation of Tin Can Island Port and the Lagos Port Complex.
President Tinubu has repeatedly defended his administration’s borrowing decisions, arguing that loans are necessary to finance critical infrastructure and other development projects.
In April, he said his administration would continue to borrow whenever necessary, insisting that borrowing should not be viewed negatively.
Mr Tinubu spoke at the State House during a meeting with Plateau State leaders led by Governor Caleb Mutfwang and the APC National Chairman, Nentawe Yilwatda.
“If we have to borrow, we borrow. Borrowing is not leprosy, we just have to work hard to be able to pay for it,” the president had said.
